rules.title: Pointee-type alternation
rules.statement: A pointee type (target of `&`/`*`/etc.) is one of: ref-type, array type, tuple type, unit type, qualified associated type, associated-type reference, fn-pointer type, or a simple type reference.

rules.title: Closure type `|T,...| -> R`
rules.statement: `|T1, T2, ...| -> R` is a closure type (parameter-type annotation position). `|| -> R` (zero-arg) is a distinct alternative because the lexer fuses `||` into one token.

rules.title: Bare fn-pointer type `fn(...) -> R`
rules.statement: `fn(T1, T2, ...) -> R` / `fn(T1, T2, ...)` / `fn() -> R` / `fn()` is a bare function-pointer type; omitted return defaults to no declared return type.

rules.title: extern-ABI fn-pointer type
rules.statement: `extern "ABI" fn(...) -> R` is a fn-pointer type carrying an ABI string; sema tags the FnPtr type with it and threads it to the MLIR calling convention (mirrors the extern-fn declaration convention).

rules.title: unsafe fn-pointer type
rules.statement: `unsafe fn(...) -> R` is a fn-pointer type with IS_UNSAFE set; otherwise structurally identical to the safe fn-pointer type. Must be tried before the bare (non-`unsafe`) alternatives so `unsafe` is consumed here.

rules.title: HRTB-quantified fn-pointer type
rules.statement: `for<'a> fn(&'a T) -> R` is a HRTB-quantified fn-pointer type; the `for<>` binders are parsed and captured (HRTB_BINDERS) but sema does not yet skolemize per-type binders — captured for future region inference.
rules.uncertainty: Binders are parsed/captured but not yet semantically enforced (per source comment); observable effect is limited to successful parsing today.

rules.title: Statement repeat-group `#(stmt)*`
rules.statement: `#(stmt)*` at statement position is a metaprogram repeat-group over a statement, expanding to a compile-time-repeated sequence of statements (mirrors the analogous repeat-group forms in type-argument and pattern-group positions).

rules.title: Unsafe block
rules.statement: `unsafe { ... }` is an unsafe block whose body is an ordinary block.

rules.title: Block
rules.statement: A block is `{ stmt* }`: a brace-delimited sequence of zero or more statements.

rules.title: Nested function statement
rules.statement: A `fn name(params) [-> T] { ... }` at statement position is a nested function: its body is lifted to a top-level free function under a gensym'd name, and the local name binds a fn-pointer value. A nested fn captures nothing; reads of enclosing locals are rejected by sema (use a closure instead).

rules.title: At-binding pattern
rules.statement: `name @ subpat` binds `name` to the value matched by `subpat`. `ref name @ subpat` binds `name` by reference to the value matched by `subpat`; this alternative is ordered before the bare `ref name` alternative so the trailing `@ subpat` is not left unparsed.

rules.title: Parenthesised / grouped pattern
rules.statement: `(P)` is exactly P. `(P | Q | ...)` is a grouped or-pattern, inlined into the same PAT_OR shape as a bare or-pattern at that position (composes with `@`-bindings, e.g. `n @ (1 | 2 | 3)`). `(..)` matches any tuple irrefutably, binding nothing (lowered as a bare wildcard).

rules.title: Byte-string pattern rejected
rules.statement: A byte-string-literal pattern parses (PAT_BYTES) but sema currently rejects it, pending &[u8]-equality-matching codegen.
rules.uncertainty: Rejection is stated as provisional ("until codegen ... lands"); reflects current compiler behavior, not necessarily a permanent restriction.

rules.title: Float-literal pattern rejected
rules.statement: A float-literal pattern (PAT_FLOAT) parses successfully but is rejected by sema with a diagnostic: float-equality matching in patterns is deliberately not supported because IEEE float-equality semantics as a pattern are not committed to.
rules.divergence: Rust historically deprecated float patterns (accept-with-lint); Logos rejects them outright with a hard diagnostic.

rules.title: Integer literal patterns
rules.statement: In a pattern position, `N` matches a scrutinee equal to the integer literal `N` (PAT_INT); `-N` matches equal to the negative integer literal `-N` (PAT_NEG_INT).

rules.title: String-literal pattern
rules.statement: A string-literal pattern `"foo"` matches by string equality; sema lowers it to a refutable `str_eq(scrutinee, "foo")` guard over a wildcard binding.

rules.title: Or-pattern
rules.statement: A top-level pattern is one or more `pat_single` alternatives separated by `|` (optional leading `|`), combined into a single or-pattern (PAT_OR). A variant-payload argument may itself be an or-pattern `Some(A | B)` — PAT_OR is emitted there only when a `|` is actually present; a single alternative unwraps/passes through transparently.

rules.title: Char patterns
rules.statement: A char literal pattern `'a'` matches a char value; `'a'..='z'` matches an inclusive char range over char values.

rules.title: Integer range patterns
rules.statement: Integer range patterns: closed inclusive `lo..=hi`, closed exclusive `lo..hi`, and half-open forms `a..` (RangeFrom, clamped to [a, TYPE_MAX]), `..=b` (RangeToInclusive, clamped to [TYPE_MIN, b]), `..b` (RangeToExclusive, clamped to [TYPE_MIN, b-1]). Either endpoint may independently carry a unary `-` (negative literal). Open bounds are clamped to the scrutinee type's MIN/MAX when the pattern is built.

rules.title: ref / ref mut / mut bindings
rules.statement: `ref x` binds the matched place by shared reference; `ref mut x` by mutable reference; `mut x` introduces a fresh re-bindable mutable local from the scrutinee (by value).

rules.title: Reference patterns
rules.statement: `&pat` and `&mut pat` match a reference, peeling one scrutinee reference layer (built as PAT_REF). Because the lexer fuses `&&` into a single AND token, `&&pat` / `&&mut pat` cannot reach the `AMP …` alternatives directly; instead the grammar matches AND followed by an inner reference and wraps it once more, peeling two layers and producing PAT_REF(PAT_REF(pat)) — each PAT_REF still peels exactly one scrutinee reference layer.

rules.title: Slice pattern
rules.statement: `[elems]` / `[]` match a slice/array by element sub-patterns.

rules.title: Struct-pattern field
rules.statement: A struct-pattern field is one of: `..` (rest), `N: subpat` (tuple-struct field by positional integer index N, resolved positionally by sema's struct-pattern binder), `name: subpat`, `ref name` / `ref mut name` (bind the field by reference, `&T` / `&mut T`), or a bare `name` shorthand binding the field to a same-named local.

rules.title: Struct pattern
rules.statement: `Name { field_list }` and `Name {}` destructure a struct by named fields: `Name { field_list }` binds/matches the listed fields (via pat_field_list); `Name {}` matches a struct with no field bindings.

rules.title: Let-binding tuple pattern
rules.statement: A let-binding tuple pattern (`pat_binding`) admits `()` (unit), a `..` rest (expanded at lowering to the right number of `_` skips so the remaining names land on the correct tuple slots), nested tuples `(a, (b, c))` (the sub-list is stored under NAMES, the same shape as LET_DESTRUCT, so the sema let-destructure lowering recurses into it), and plain identifier bindings.

rules.title: Tuple-pattern rest element
rules.statement: A tuple-pattern element (`pat_tuple_elem`) is either `..` (rest — later lowered to a `_` wildcard skip, preserving the tuple's fixed arity) or an or-pattern of one or more sub-patterns (`pat_single (PIPE pat_single)*`, emitted as `PAT_OR`).

rules.title: Enum struct-variant pattern
rules.statement: `E::V { x, y: pat, .. }` / `E::V {}` match a struct-shaped enum variant; field names resolve to variant payload indices via payload_field_names.

rules.title: Enum tuple-variant / tuple-struct pattern
rules.statement: `E::V(args)` matches an enum tuple-variant payload; `args` are full nested patterns, possibly including `..` rest and or-patterns (CODE: PAT_VARIANT_DATA, NAME, FIELD, ARGS). A bare `Foo(a, b)` (no `::` separator) also parses as CODE: PAT_VARIANT_DATA with an empty FIELD; sema then dispatches to tuple-struct destructure vs. enum-variant destructure based on how `Foo` resolves.

rules.title: Identifier / wildcard pattern
rules.statement: A bare identifier is an irrefutable binding pattern: the matched value is bound to the name. `_` is lexed as an ordinary identifier and treated by sema as the anonymous wildcard (binds nothing).

rules.title: Writ map/array patterns
rules.statement: `@{ "key": pat, ... }` / `@{}` match writ maps (keys are string literals); `@[elem, ...]` / `@[]` match writ arrays. Array elements admit a trailing `..` to match length >= n.

rules.title: Writ scalar patterns
rules.statement: `@null`, `@true`/`@false`, `@N`/`@-N`, and `@"str"` are writ scalar patterns matching writ null, bool, integer, and string values respectively.

rules.title: Writ typed map/array patterns
rules.statement: `@<T>{..}`, `@<K,V>{..}`, and `@<T>[..]` are typed writ map/array patterns annotating the matched container's element type(s).

rules.title: break
rules.statement: `break;`, `break expr;`, `break 'label;`, and `break 'label expr;` are all valid; a value and/or a target label are each optional. A bare `break` (no label, no value) may be terminated by either `;` or `,`.

rules.title: continue
rules.statement: `continue;` and `continue 'label;` are valid; the target label is optional. A bare (unlabeled) `continue` may be terminated by either `;` or `,`.

rules.title: For-each loop
rules.statement: `for x in iter { }` iterates over an iterable, binding the loop variable per element. If the loop variable is a bare identifier, the fast-path alternative binds it directly (tried first). If it is not a bare identifier (a tuple/struct/etc. pattern, e.g. `for (a, b) in v { }`), the parser falls through to the pattern alternative, and sema binds the full destructuring pattern against each element.

rules.title: For-range loop
rules.statement: `for i in lo..hi { }` iterates the exclusive integer range `[lo, hi)`; `for i in lo..=hi { }` iterates the inclusive range `[lo, hi]`.

rules.title: Statement forms
rules.statement: A statement is one of: repeat-group (`#(stmt)*`), nested-fn, labeled-loop, let-else, let, for, while, loop, return, break, continue, deref-write, if-expr, match, destructure-assign, assign, compound-assign, place-assign, unsafe-block, block, `expr ;` (expression statement), or a trailing `expr` (block-tail value, becomes the block's value with no `;`).

rules.title: let-else statement
rules.statement: `let PAT = expr else { block };` binds a refutable pattern; on match failure the else block runs (must diverge — the pattern's bindings are otherwise unavailable after the statement).

rules.title: let bindings
rules.statement: `let` supports: tuple destructure `let (a,b) [: T] = e;`; `let ref x [: T] = e;` (sugar for `let x = &e;` — detected via IS_REF, sema wraps the lowered RHS in an addr-of); `let mut x [: T] [= e];` (mutable; `let mut x: T;` with no initializer declares an uninitialized typed mutable binding); `let x [: T] [= e];` (immutable; `let x: T;` likewise declares an uninitialized typed binding); and `let PAT = e;` (arbitrary irrefutable full pattern — struct/enum-variant/tuple-with-non-ident-subs — for forms not covered by the simpler IDENT-prefixed alternatives above; refutability is checked at sema time).

rules.title: loop block
rules.statement: `loop { ... }` is an unconditional loop.

rules.title: Labeled loop
rules.statement: `'label: for/while/loop { ... }` attaches a lifetime-syntax label to a loop (in statement or expression position), targetable by `break 'label` / `continue 'label` to disambiguate nested loops.

rules.title: Match arm with optional guard
rules.statement: A match arm is `PAT [if GUARD] => BODY [,]`, where BODY is a block, an expression, or a statement, with an optional trailing comma. The optional `if GUARD` is a boolean guard expression gating the arm.

rules.title: Match statement
rules.statement: `match SCRUT { ARM* }` matches a scrutinee against arms. A bare-identifier scrutinee is parsed specially (as a var-ref) so `match e { ... }` does not mis-parse `e {` as a struct literal; complex scrutinee expressions fall through to the general expr form.

rules.title: Array size from metacall block
rules.statement: `[T; metacall { ... }]` computes the array size from a metacall block evaluated at compile time (const array-length is expressed via explicit `metacall`, not implicit const-eval).

rules.title: Array size from variadic pack length
rules.statement: `[T; P...(P)]` sizes the array from a variadic pack's length; lowered to a symbolic array-size-var `__sizeof_pack:P`, resolved at monomorphization.

rules.title: Fixed-size array type `[T; N]`
rules.statement: `[T; N]` is a fixed-size array type. N may be an integer literal, an identifier (const generic), a variadic-pack-length form `sizeof...(P)` (lowered to a symbolic arr_size_var resolved at mono), or a `metacall { ... }` block computing the size. All size-bearing alternatives are tried before the unsized-slice fallback `[T]`; PEG alternation is ordered left-to-right so size-bearing forms always match first when a size is present.

rules.title: Generic type instantiation `T<...>`
rules.statement: `Name<arg, ...>` (optional trailing comma) instantiates a generic type. The type name may also be a metavariable: `#Ident<...>` or `#(expr)<...>`.

rules.title: Generic type-argument kinds
rules.statement: A generic type argument is one of: a repeat-group `#(arg),*` (metaprogram repetition over type args), a lifetime `'a` (stored as LIFETIME_PARAM, skipped during concrete-type resolution), a pack expansion `Ident...`, an antiquote `$Ident` or `$Ident...`, an integer literal (optionally negated), a writ literal, or a plain type.

rules.title: Raw pointer type
rules.statement: `*const T` is an immutable raw pointer to `T`; `*mut T` is a mutable raw pointer to `T`.

rules.title: Raw fat-pointer to slice
rules.statement: `*const [T]` and `*mut [T]` are raw fat pointers to a slice, sharing the `{*const T, usize}` ABI of `&[T]` but without borrow-check guarantees. These alternatives must precede the plain pointer/array forms in `ptr_type` so that a bare `[T]` still parses as the unsized-slice type rather than falling through to `arr_type` (which requires `[T; N]` with an explicit size).

rules.title: Zoned raw pointer `*zoned [mut] T`
rules.statement: `*zoned T` / `*zoned mut T` is a zoned raw pointer (Ref-arm self-relative at rest; deref/assign runs the storage↔compute bridge). `zoned` is a contextual keyword recognized only in pointer position: after `*`, the only words otherwise valid there are the `mut`/`const` keyword tokens, so a bare IDENT there can only be `zoned` (sema validates NAME=="zoned"). It is not reserved globally — `#[zoned]` attributes still parse as IDENT.
rules.divergence: A6 (addition — zone-relative raw pointer; no Rust equivalent; ref-repr-design §6/§8)

rules.title: Fully-qualified non-generic type path
rules.statement: A fully-qualified non-generic type in type position is written `pkg.path.Type` (dotted); the last path segment is the type name (QUAL_PARTS holds the prefix). Matched before bare-IDENT alternatives so the whole dotted form is claimed as one type reference. The generic dotted form `pkg.path.Type<A>` is not accepted here (use a `use` import + short name instead).

rules.title: Metavariable type reference
rules.statement: `#Ident` and `#(expr)` are (non-generic) type references whose name is supplied by a metaprogram variable/expression rather than a literal identifier.

rules.title: Unit type `()`
rules.statement: `()` denotes the unit type, the empty tuple type; both the dedicated unit-type production and the simple-type `LPAREN RPAREN` fallback yield the same TUPLE_TYPE (no items).
